newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia race row MP could help Howard.
newsitem.headline: Australia race row MP could help Howard.

text.p: At first glance, the surging popularity of race row MP Pauline Hanson should be a threat to Australia's conservative prime minister, John Howard.

Beset by political problems ranging from Aboriginal land claims to corruption, the last thing Howard might have wanted to hear this week was that Hanson's fledgling One Nation party was scoring 10 percent in opinion polls.

But political analysts said on Wednesday that far from threatening Howard, Hanson could actually prove his greatest asset over the next 18 months or so by giving him the lever he needs to force reforms through a hostile parliament.
According to their analysis, no party in the upper house Senate will want to block government legislation and force Howard into a snap election while Hanson was still riding high.
"None of those Senate parties are going to want a couple of Hansonites into the Senate, are they?," said Malcolm Mackerras, an electoral specialist at the Australian Defence Force Acadamy.
"Pauline Hanson is doing John Howard's dirty work for him, basically. This is actually a weapon in the hand of Howard."

Two polls on Wednesday showed Hanson was rapidly winning supporters for her far-right One Nation Party -- enough to give her a strong chance of an influential role in parliament in the right circumstances.
Most analysts and political leaders say the inexperienced fish-and-chip shop owner will fade away, like other populists before her, by the next election due by early 1999.
"It won't last," Mackerras told Reuters. "It's got 18 months to wither on the vine, and I've got no doubt it will wither on the vine."
Howard himself said voters would realise Hanson's simplistic policies would not solve their problems and mid-term opinion polls counted for little.
"We are living at the moment at a time of tremendous change and upheaval and people feel uncertain, they feel insecure," he said in a radio interview.
Australian National University political scientist David Jupp said Hanson's support was grounded in the conservative nature of her home state, Australia's "Deep North".

"It's a Queensland phenomenon to a very large extent," Jupp told Reuters. "There's been these messiahs ... in the last 10 years. All sort of right-wing knights or maidens on white horses with very big poll support, which all disappeared again."

But in the meantime, Hanson's popularity and the consequent threat to established parties gave the Liberal-National government a weapon to use in a Senate where it is two seats short of a majority and where coming battles include the passage of the next budget, due in two weeks.

With One Nation's support running high enough to win more than one Senate seat in a double dissolution election, the non-government parties would pass government legislation to avoid a trigger for an early poll.
If the Senate twice rejects government legislation, both houses of parliament can be dissolved for an early election, followed by a joint sitting to debate the rejected bills.
Usually, only half of the Senate faces each election and the Senate's peculiar voting system means fewer votes are needed to win a seat if all Senate places are up for election.

"It's far better for him (Howard) to allow the threat of Hanson to guarantee that the Senate doesn't create triggers for a double dissolution for fear that he might actually pull a trigger and that will suddenly admit to the Senate a couple of Hansonites," Mackerras said.

Hanson, dumped by Howard's Liberals before the last election over controversial comments about Asians and Aborigines, is campaigning on an end to immigration, reduced foreign investment and renewed trade barriers.

She sparked a divisive national race row last year when she warned Australia was in danger of being over-run by Asians and complained that Aborigines were being given special treatment at the expense of white Australians.
One Nation director David Ettridge said Hanson was popular because the major parties were no longer listening to "mainstream Australia".

"At the same time that Canberra is self-destructing, with the integrity of politicians at an all-time low, Pauline is a fresh face, she speaks her mind, she identifies with mainstream Australia -- and she speaks the truth," Ettridge told Reuters.
